content:
I argue that we should use the one that is more suitable for the binary search tree algorithm. See the discussion here.

I don't think a different argument order is a good reason to throw out Tree (edit: nor I see does Chris in the PR)

I don't want to throw out, but I want to emphasize a different representation of a tree definition. For AI, there would be no difference, but for humans, there would be. It is very different. Each definition has their own advantage in the task at hand. We should not stick to the "first" definition.

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai said:

I don't want to throw out, but I want to emphasize a different representation of a tree definition. For AI, there would be no difference, but for humans, there would be. It is very different.

What is different besides the order of constructors?
Ergonomics

We should not stick to the "first" definition.

On the contrary; a huge reason mathlib is successful is that it tries as hard as possible to have one true definition. Consistency is far more valuable than matching the exact style used by every author at the expense of duplication
Sure that's for mathlib. But we can be consistent for data structure throughout.
I encourage you to try to think about formalizing BSTs, and maybe you may feel some friction with a "wrong" representation.
In-order traversal gives you a sorted list. Very easy to visualize.

Repeating context from the PR, the objection is that

def rotateLeft : BinaryTree α → BinaryTree α
| .node a x (.node b y c) => .node (.node a x b) y c
| t => t

is easier to read than

def rotateLeft : Tree α → Tree α
| .node x a (.node y b c) => .node y (.node x a b) c
| t => t

If you really want this, you can define

@[match_pattern] abbrev Tree.node' (a x b) := Tree.node x a b

I value a good definition that allows us to formalize things easily. Will that create fragmentation? There is a reason one representation is better than the other. I can only see from the points of data structure. I won't say that in-order is always canonical choice.

I want to mention that in general, a binary tree can be represented in pre-order, in-order, and post-order. They are different depending on tasks at hand. I can see that post-order is good for path-compression type arguments. in-order is good for binary search trees. Pre-order (not sure, but I am sure Mathlib has good reason for it).
Thanks for the suggestion. I'll try!

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai said:

Sure that's for mathlib. But we can be consistent for data structure throughout.

I very strongly disagree here. We've deliberately decided to not replicate definitions that already exist in Mathlib unless we are making a generalization or for larger changes like computability. Changing the order of constructors does not fit in with this.

I want to mention that in general, a binary tree can be represented in pre-order, in-order, and post-order.

I don't believe this. A binary tree can be _serialized_ in three orders, but that's not the canonical representation which is unordered
I am talking about the definition of binary tree.

I don't agree with the way you are using the word "representation". If a mathematician said "a bijection is a pair of forward and reverse function" and you interrupted with "no, it's a pair of a reverse and forward function", then they would dismiss you as wasting their time. This is exactly how users of CSLib will feel when presented with both Tree and BinaryTree with the only difference being ordering.

Eric Wieser said:

I don't agree with the way you are using the word "representation". If a mathematician said "a bijection is a pair of forward and reverse function" and you interrupted with "no, it's a pair of a reverse and forward function", then they would dismiss you as wasting their time. This is exactly how users of CSLib will feel when presented with both Tree and BinaryTree with the only difference being ordering.

I am happy to try this
@[match_pattern] abbrev Tree.node' (a x b) := Tree.node x a b

But the name node' is a bit strange.
To be clear: if you truly believe that .node a x b is the globally better spelling, then a way to proceed would be to modify the definition in mathlib to use this order instead

The fact this matches docs#Lean.RBNode does seem like a reasonable argument (even if this is to ultimately be dropped from Lean)

(Lean.RBNode α β ≃ Tree (Lean.RBColor × Σ a, β a) is true, IIUC)

Absolutely, for binary search tree yes. It is about ordering. When you declare, .node a x b, you see that everything in a is at most x and everything in b is at least x. This property (nice ordering) still holds when you unfold multiple times. In mathlib, binary tree is an abstract object. The default definition seems to be that way. I don't have a strong opinion on what's in Mathlib.

Thinking again, I think this is all a distraction and the solution is notation:

import Mathlib

/-- A tree node -/
notation:65 l:66 " △[" v "] " r:66 => Tree.node v l r

def rotateLeft : Tree α → Tree α
  | a △[x] (b △[y] c) => (a △[x] b) △[y] c
  | t => t
(mathlib already has a △ b notation for node-less trees)
24 messages were moved here from #CSLib > Splay tree PR by Eric Wieser.
Happy to try this solution, but the info-view will unfold △ notations, right? Is there a way to keep △ notation in the info-view?
Yes, if you take my code and then do nothing to it, then △ will be preserved in the infoview
You might be thinking of syntax instead of notation; syntax does not write delaborators for you.
(admittedly notation doesn't always write a delaborator if your notation expands to something complex)
Can I just declare syntax and use it with ease? Will it complicate the proof?
Do you mean notation?
Right. Sorry

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai said:

I am talking about the definition of binary tree.

Incorrect/not related. A binary tree does not impose such order. As Eric says those are different linearisations. None of this is affected by constructor argument order.

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai said:

Can I just declare notation and use it with ease? Will it complicate the proof?

The key thing here is that using a different structure BinaryTree (or abbrev node') means your theorem statements are genuinely different (in a type-theoretic sense) from the alternative spelling. When you use notation, the underlying object is identical, as the notation is just in the parsing layer.
In mathlib, Tree is defined as a binary tree. But this name is misleading. I prefer the name binary tree.
That's a fair criticism of mathlib; would you mind making a PR to mathlib to rename it?
Sure will do!

Quick update on this: for now the PR keeps its own BinaryTree.lean (the in-order version) and imports that. Sorrachai is currently working on updating the tree on the Mathlib side, so the plan is to move over to the Mathlib one once that's ready instead of carrying our own copy.
It looks like the PR has already been updated to use Mathlib.Data.Tree.Basic in BinaryTree.lean, correct? (To be clear this is good, but confused me comparing the above message and the code)

Yes, this is correct: the PR builds on Mathlib.Data.Tree.Basic, not a separate type. Sorry the earlier message was misleading.

To be precise: we add some general operations on top of Mathlib's tree (membership, in-order traversal, the △[] notation, plus rotations and IsBST). Several of those are exactly what Sorrachai is upstreaming. That is the Tree → BinaryTree rename in https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/39707, and the Membership instance, △[] notation and traversals in https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/39697 (the △[] there is the same definition we use here).

Once those land we can switch to BinaryTree and drop our local copies, and the file name will line up with the rename. The △[] is just notation; the underlying constructor is Mathlib's key-first node.
